items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Sea otters maintain entire underwater forests
items.claim: Where sea otters live, kelp forests thrive. Where they have been hunted to near-extinction, sea urchins explode and graze kelp to bare rock ('urchin barrens'). One otter eats about 25% of its body mass in urchins daily.
items.prompt: What makes otters a keystone species?

options.text: They are the largest predators present
They selectively eat sea urchins, the only major kelp grazer in the system; removing otters releases urchin populations, which devastate kelp forests that support hundreds of other species
Otters fertilise the water with their waste

items.reveal:
Jim Estes and John Palmisano (1974) compared Aleutian islands with otters to islands where otters had been wiped out for the fur trade. The contrast was startling: lush kelp forests vs barren urchin-grazed rock.

Kelp forests are enormously productive. They support fish, invertebrates, sea birds, marine mammals. They sequester carbon. They dampen wave energy and protect coasts.

Subsequent work (Estes et al. 1998) suggested that killer whale predation on sea otters — possibly because their normal prey, large whales, had been depleted by whaling — was driving a SECOND collapse of Aleutian otter populations, with knock-on collapses of kelp.

A whaling-era extinction cascade may still be propagating decades later. Ecosystems have memory.

The 'keystone species' concept (Paine 1969) was based on starfish; otters became its most famous illustration. Many ecosystems have keystones; identifying them before they collapse is a recurring conservation challenge.
items.why: Big effects from one species seem improbable. In sea otter ecosystems, the entire architecture depends on one mid-sized predator preventing one herbivore from grazing the forest down.

items.title: Remove three quarters of a liver and it grows back
items.claim: Humans can lose 70-75% of their liver (in surgery or donation) and regrow it to original size within weeks. The liver is the only solid human organ with this level of regenerative ability. Even other strongly regenerative tissues (skin, bone marrow) can't grow back this much organ.

options.text: A reservoir of liver stem cells expands

Mature hepatocytes (normally quiescent) re-enter the cell cycle and divide; growth factors (HGF, EGF, IL-6) signal the remaining cells to proliferate until the original organ mass is restored, then stop
Surrounding organs grow into the missing space
The bile duct generates new liver tissue

items.reveal:
Normal adult liver: hepatocytes (~80% of liver cells) sit in G0, dividing at most once every year or two. Cellular workhorses doing biochemistry, not growing.

After partial hepatectomy (surgical removal): within hours, growth factors (hepatocyte growth factor HGF, EGF, TGF-alpha) surge in the portal blood. Hepatocytes enter S phase by 24-48 hours, divide, and continue dividing until liver mass returns. Then they switch off and resume their quiescent state.

Full regeneration in 2-3 weeks. Donors who give part of their liver for transplant recover their original liver mass and function.

Limit: the regeneration requires intact liver remnant. Cirrhotic livers — where hepatocytes have been replaced by scar tissue — cannot regenerate. Acute liver failure with widespread cell death may also overwhelm the regenerative response.

The Prometheus myth (vulture eats his liver, which regrows nightly) suggests ancient Greek anatomists may have noticed liver regeneration. Modern molecular understanding mostly dates from the 1980s-90s.

The liver's regenerative capacity is one of the foundations of living donor transplants — a partial donation to a recipient leaves both with functional livers.
items.why: Major organ regrowth seems out of reach for mammals. The liver does it routinely — and the molecular signals are now well enough understood to be co-opted for transplant medicine.
